doc.title: Javon Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: George Floyd protests and a police stop in New Jersey
summary: Jackson discusses the global protests and recounts being questioned by police while parked in a Mercedes.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It makes me wonder if historians or even ten years from now, when they think of the spring of 2020, we already had a political crisis going on, at least in my estimation, and we have a pandemic, and now we have this racial crisis spawned by this incident in Minneapolis. And I don’t have a question here I guess I’m just wondering if you think that this particular time will result in some significant change.

I think that this most recent situation, murder of George Floyd, has ignited in a way that I’ve never seen, and even if you look at a lot of the protests, and most of all I’ve found all the protests in the past that have erupted from cities have been because of the police or the killing of a black person. So you see it over in parts of Europe or London, so it has really spread in a way that you would have never seen it before. And I think that some of the things I’m seeing — I saw something last night on the road or bridge in Portland, Oregon, they just laid on the ground and took up the whole bridge, and the fact that the other protests if you will, they were largely African-American or black people. Now you are seeing there is an interracial group. It’s not all just — there’s a lot of white people involved that are marching that really feel outraged and it’s really getting the attention of a lot of people, where there’s more meaningful conversation to understand what Javon, for example, do you experience racism every day? Absolutely. You think about things in a different way and so it’s finally — the powder keg has really popped and so we really have to have a conversation in a way you can really get to understanding, well Javon had never been stopped over by the police possibly because you’re black. Well I was sitting in a parking lot some years ago in New Jersey, in Fawn Park, New Jersey. I was to meet my wife at a Trader Joe’s. We were going to meet at noon but I was early, I got there © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

about 11:30, 11:35, and within about three minutes, five minutes, someone knocked on my windshield. And I looked to my left, it was a policeman. He said, “I’m just getting a response from one of the stores in this area” it was like a little mall, “that you’ve been sitting here for a few minutes. Could I ask why?” I said, “Well it’s really none of your business.” He says, “Well I want to see your driver’s license and registration.” So I had a couple of choices. Because we always have a choice. I could make a big deal out of it or I could show him what he wants. Well here’s the thing, okay Javon Jackson’s in a Mercedes. Really? That’s basically what it was. It this his car? Let’s find out, is it stolen? And so I handed him the driver’s license and registration. Of course it checked out, he handed it back. So I always laugh, that wasn’t even a driving while black. That was, I was parked, that’s something that you would never have to go through. No one would see you in a Mercedes and question if it’s your car. So these kinds of things happen all the time, regularly.
